HOLLM is an intuitive and practically relevant combination of adaptive KD-tree partitioning, region-level exploration/exploitation scoring, and localized LLM proposals.

The evaluation covers continuous synthetic functions, hyperparameter optimization, and neural architecture search, and consistently includes a global-LLM baseline using the same nominal proposal count.

The appendix supplies pseudocode, prompts, benchmark descriptions, hyperparameter sensitivity experiments, and a component ablation; the limitations and societal-impact discussion is appropriately candid.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence is not sufficiently reliable for the strong claims: most main experiments use only three runs, provide no statistical tests or numerical result tables, and rely chiefly on visually comparing highly variable learning curves. NAS uses six runs, but this does not resolve the broader issue.

Reproducibility is poor. The promised repository URL is absent, while the proprietary LLM is identified only as Gemini-1.5-Flash without an exact model/API version, decoding parameters, retry and parsing procedures, treatment of invalid or duplicate candidates, or complete cost and latency measurements.

The algorithm is internally underspecified. With five initial observations, leaf capacity ceil(d/2), and M=5, several experiments initially have fewer than five KD-tree leaves, making the stated selection of five distinct leaves without replacement impossible. The detailed pseudocode instead appears to sample categorically without specifying replacement. Min-max normalization in degenerate cases and precise derivation of cell boundaries are also undefined.

The comparison does not control computational resources. HOLLM makes five separate LLM calls with repeated context per round, whereas the global LLM apparently makes one call producing the same number of candidates; token usage, latency, and monetary cost are not matched or reported. The classical baselines are vastly cheaper, so evaluation-count parity alone is inadequate.

The central benchmark results may exploit memorized structural priors rather than demonstrate general black-box optimization. The especially striking recovery of the exact optimum on standard Ackley-20D is not validated on shifted, rotated, procedurally generated, or otherwise held-out functions. Such tests are important when the optimizer is a pretrained model potentially exposed to these canonical benchmarks.

Novelty is moderate: the contribution primarily combines standard KD-tree partitioning, heuristic bandit-style region scoring, and an LLM sampler. There is no theoretical analysis, and the proposed score is only loosely inspired by UCB-V; because log(t/(K_t n_l)) is zero for cells sampled at or above the average occupancy, standard optimism or regret interpretations do not directly apply.

The ablations are too narrow to substantiate the design. The component study is shown only on one NAS task, hyperparameter studies use one synthetic problem or four FCNet tasks, and there is no broad comparison against alternative partitioning schemes or stronger modern high-dimensional optimization methods. Consequently, it remains unclear which elaborate scoring components generalize beyond the reported settings.

Several claims are overstated or insufficiently documented, including “consistently outperforming” state-of-the-art methods and the Hausdorff-distance coverage experiment, whose approximation over a continuous hypercube, repetitions, and uncertainty are not specified. Overall, the idea is promising, but substantial experimental and reproducibility work is needed for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and intuitive combination of adaptive KD-tree partitioning, bandit-inspired region scoring, and localized LLM candidate generation.

The empirical study covers continuous optimization, hyperparameter optimization, and neural architecture search, with comparisons to several established Bayesian-optimization and evolutionary baselines.
The paper includes useful component and hyperparameter ablations, full pseudocode, prompt templates, and an explicit discussion of limitations and societal impact.
weaknesses: The novelty is modest: the method primarily combines established spatial partitioning, UCB-style scoring, and LLM sampling. Crucially, it is not compared against the most directly relevant partition-based optimizers such as HOO, adaptive-treed bandits, DIRECT-style methods, or LaMCTS, making it difficult to attribute gains to the proposed contribution.

The evaluation is statistically weak. Most results use only three runs, provide no significance tests or numerical result tables, and rely mainly on visually overlapping learning curves. The component ablation is restricted to one NAS task, while hyperparameter ablations are similarly narrow.

The synthetic evaluation uses canonical, unshifted benchmark functions whose optima and structure may occur in LLM training data. In particular, results such as rapidly finding the origin on Ackley cannot establish general black-box reasoning without shifted, rotated, procedurally generated, or otherwise contamination-resistant functions.

The comparison is not compute-equivalent: HOLLM makes multiple separate LLM calls over localized regions, while the global LLM baseline appears to generate all candidates in one call. Matching the number of proposals does not control inference calls, tokens, latency, or monetary cost, none of which are reported. It is therefore unclear whether gains arise from partitioning or simply additional inference and diversity from repeated calls.

Several technical claims are unsupported or incorrect. Restricting an axis-aligned box does not make the problem lower-dimensional; stochastic selection does not imply suboptimal regions are sampled infinitely often in the finite, dynamically repartitioned procedure; and adding epsilon before min-max normalization does not guarantee every leaf a positive selection probability. The proposed score has no analysis or calibration justification, and its logarithmic UCB term becomes zero for many normally populated leaves.

Reproducibility is insufficient. The method uses a proprietary, mutable Gemini model without reporting an exact model snapshot, decoding parameters, API settings, failure-handling rules, token usage, or costs. The promised repository link is blank, and the paper is ambiguous about using one versus two prompts for generation and prediction.

There are notable algorithmic and reporting inconsistencies: the main text says leaves are sampled without replacement whereas the detailed pseudocode gives ordinary categorical sampling; the baseline proposal count is described as both k*b and k*M; T alternates between iterations and evaluations; and normalization is ambiguously placed in the detailed pseudocode.

For categorical FCNet and NAS spaces, ordinal or continuous encodings impose arbitrary neighborhood and volume structures on nominal choices. The paper does not test sensitivity to category ordering, even though KD-tree partitions and the geometric exploration score depend directly on this encoding.

Overall, the evidence does not adequately support the broad claim that HOLLM consistently matches or surpasses state-of-the-art optimization methods. The missing direct baselines, possible benchmark memorization, low run counts, and incomplete compute accounting are substantial enough to place the work below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: HOLLM presents a clear and practically motivated combination of adaptive KD-tree partitioning, bandit-inspired region selection, and localized LLM candidate generation.

The empirical scope is reasonably broad, covering six continuous synthetic functions, four hyperparameter-optimization tasks, and three NAS-Bench-201 datasets, with comparisons against GP-EI, TuRBO, TPE, BORE, CQR, regularized evolution, random search, and a global-LLM baseline.

Results consistently indicate that localization improves over otherwise similar global LLM sampling, while HOLLM is often competitive with strong conventional optimizers, including promising behavior on higher-dimensional synthetic problems.

The paper includes useful component and hyperparameter ablations, full prompt templates, detailed pseudocode, and an appropriate discussion of computational, reproducibility, and societal limitations.
The presentation is intuitive and generally well organized; the motivating sampling examples and optimization-process visualizations communicate the central idea effectively.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence is not yet sufficiently robust for an unqualified top-tier acceptance: most results use only three runs, provide curves rather than numerical summaries or statistical tests, and do not quantify sensitivity to LLM sampling randomness.

Performance is demonstrated using only Gemini-1.5-Flash. There is no optimizer study across LLM families, decoding settings, or open models, so it is unclear whether the claimed benefit is model-independent or reproducible once this proprietary model changes.

The synthetic evaluation relies on standard, unshifted functions with highly recognizable structure and often simple optimum locations. The striking Ackley-20D result is therefore difficult to disentangle from learned benchmark priors or center bias; shifted, rotated, compositional, and genuinely unknown objectives are needed.

The ablation against partitioned random or local-GP sampling appears limited to a single NAS task. Applying these controls across the benchmark suite is essential for establishing that the LLM contributes beyond the KD-tree region-selection heuristic itself.

There are algorithmic inconsistencies requiring clarification. The text specifies selecting M distinct leaves without replacement, whereas the detailed pseudocode uses categorical sampling and does not state without-replacement selection. Moreover, with five initial points and M=5, several default leaf-size settings can initially produce fewer than five leaves.

The claim that every leaf always has positive probability and hence suboptimal leaves are sampled infinitely often is not established. Min-max normalization can assign zero to all components of a leaf despite the pre-normalization epsilon, and per-round positivity alone would not imply infinite visitation under changing probabilities.

Reproducibility and efficiency reporting are incomplete: the manuscript does not report API/model version details, decoding parameters, failures or retries, wall-clock time, token usage, or monetary cost, and the stated repository link is absent from the anonymized manuscript.

The novelty is primarily a sensible integration of established partitioning, bandit scoring, and LLM proposal mechanisms rather than a fundamentally new optimization principle, and the method has no supporting regret or convergence analysis. Overall, the idea and results are promising, but the evaluation and specification gaps place it marginally below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The central motivation is compelling: localized prompting can mitigate the poor coverage and proposal collapse exhibited by globally prompted LLM optimizers.
HOLLM is clearly structured, combining adaptive KD-tree partitioning, exploitation, geometric exploration, variance-aware exploration, and localized LLM candidate generation.
The evaluation spans continuous synthetic functions, discrete hyperparameter and architecture search, engineering simulators, observation noise, and several proprietary and open-weight LLMs.
The global-LLM and random-sampling-with-KD-tree baselines, together with scoring and hyperparameter ablations, are useful attempts to isolate the contributions of localization, scoring, and the LLM.
weaknesses: The synthetic evidence is seriously vulnerable to benchmark memorization. Standard domains such as Ackley on [-32.768,32.768]^20, Rastrigin, Rosenbrock, and Levy can reveal the benchmark and its known optimizer to an LLM trained on optimization literature. HOLLM reaching the exact Ackley optimum in fewer than 50 evaluations is therefore not convincing evidence of black-box optimization on unseen functions. Randomly transformed, shifted, rotated, or newly generated functions are needed.

Experimental reliability is undermined by apparent reporting or implementation errors. In Table 4, GP-EI, regularized evolution, and random search have exactly identical means and standard errors on all three benchmarks, which is extremely unlikely. Several algorithm and prompt descriptions are also inconsistent, including k*b versus k*M proposals, generation plus prediction using separate versus unified prompts, and a malformed prediction template.

The compute-matched comparison with the global LLM baseline is unclear. HOLLM makes separate calls for M regions, whereas the global baseline appears to request all candidates in one call. Multiple independent calls can improve diversity by themselves. The complexity appendix simultaneously states that HOLLM requires M sequential requests and that both methods use the same number of inference steps. Matching candidate count alone does not match calls, tokens, latency, or sampling opportunities.

The statistical evidence is insufficient for several strong claims. Most results provide only means and standard errors; there are no paired tests or confidence intervals for final regret, and the critical-difference analysis does not specify its statistical test or significance level. Claims of significant superiority and noise robustness are consequently unsupported.

The method is largely a heuristic combination of established KD-tree partitioning, bandit-inspired scoring, and LLM sampling, with no theoretical guarantee. Moreover, the claimed bandit interpretation is overstated: min-max normalization does not ensure every region has positive probability, stochastic finite-horizon selection does not imply regions are sampled infinitely often, and the proposed UCB-V expression is not justified for dynamically refitted regions.

Reproducibility is weak: the promised repository link is absent, important API settings and invalid-output handling are unspecified, and the pseudocode disagrees about whether T counts rounds or evaluations and how it is incremented. These ambiguities materially affect evaluation budgets.

Most component ablations are conducted on only one or two tasks, and the comparisons to strong partitioning optimizers are relegated to low-repetition appendix experiments. The surrogate-calibration analysis is imported from a follow-up paper and does not establish that calibration causes the optimization gains reported here.

strengths: The core intuition—using adaptive spatial partitioning to make LLM candidate generation more local—is sensible and potentially useful.
The evaluation covers synthetic optimization, hyperparameter optimization, engineering benchmarks, multiple LLMs, and several ablations.
Including a global-LLM baseline and a random-sampling-with-KD-tree baseline is directionally appropriate for separating localization from LLM effects.
The paper provides pseudocode, prompts, runtime/cost estimates, and a candid limitations and societal-impact discussion.
weaknesses: The algorithm is not consistently or completely specified. Sampling M distinct leaves is impossible during early rounds when K_t<M; min-max normalization is undefined when a component is constant; the treatment of degenerate cells is unspecified; and the text alternates between KD-tree cell boundaries and extrema of points within a leaf, which do not generally define a partition covering the search domain.

The purported UCB-V term has weak technical justification. Because t/(K_t n_l) compares a cell count with the average count, its logarithm is zero for every cell at or above average and often for nearly all balanced KD-tree leaves. Thus the variance-aware bonus can vanish systematically and is not a conventional confidence bound. No regret or consistency result supports the bandit interpretation.

The reported baseline results contain a major credibility problem: Table 4 gives exactly identical means and standard errors for GP-EI, regularized evolution, random search, and TPE on all three benchmarks. This is extraordinarily unlikely and strongly suggests an implementation or reporting error, undermining the central empirical evidence.

The comparison does not control LLM computation fairly. HOLLM makes M sequential generation requests and apparently additional prediction requests, each repeating the full history, whereas the global baseline can generate all candidates in one request. The claim that both require the same number of inference steps contradicts the described algorithms; equal candidate counts do not imply equal calls, input tokens, latency, or cost.

The striking result of locating the exact 20-dimensional Ackley optimum in fewer than 50 evaluations is not convincingly evidence of general black-box optimization. Standard named benchmarks have highly recognizable, centered optima, and LLMs also have strong center-point biases. Shifted, rotated, blinded, or procedurally generated functions are needed to rule out memorized structural priors and trivial midpoint proposals.

Statistical support is inadequate. Several appendix comparisons use only three or five repetitions, no hypothesis tests or confidence intervals for pairwise differences are reported, and the critical-difference diagram lacks enough methodological detail to verify its construction. Claims such as “significant” and “consistently outperforms” are stronger than the presented evidence.

The noise experiment is insufficiently defined: it is unclear whether incumbent quality is measured using noisy observations or latent objective values. The explanation invokes reliable mean estimation even though the exploitation statistic is explicitly a maximum and evaluations do not appear to be replicated, making the claimed robustness mechanism questionable.

Important benchmark details are missing. The multiobjective engineering problems are presented as scalar tasks without clearly defining scalarization, constraints, or objective implementations. Ordinally encoding categorical FCNet choices also imposes arbitrary KD-tree geometry whose sensitivity is not examined.

The surrogate analysis is not persuasive: it is imported directly from a separate follow-up paper, apparently uses adaptively collected and potentially incomparable evaluation sets, and reports catastrophically poor GP/TabPFN results that suggest inadequate configuration or scaling. Moreover, the global LLM has better predictive metrics than localized HOLLM on multiple tasks, contradicting parts of the accompanying interpretation.

Novelty is limited to combining established KD-tree partitioning, heuristic bandit scoring, and LLM candidate generation. Given the lack of theory, the contribution would require especially reliable empirical validation, which the inconsistencies above prevent.

Reproducibility remains limited: the repository link is absent, and API version/date, decoding parameters, response-validation behavior, failure handling, seeds, and sufficient implementation details are not provided. Proprietary-model dependence further compounds this issue.

strengths: HOLLM presents a clear and practically motivated combination of adaptive KD-tree partitioning, bandit-inspired region scoring, and localized LLM candidate generation.

The evaluation is broad, covering continuous synthetic functions, discrete hyperparameter and architecture search, engineering benchmarks, observation noise, and several proprietary and open-weight LLMs.

The matched global-LLM baseline, KD-tree random-sampling baseline, scoring ablations, and comparisons with established optimizers provide useful evidence that localization and region allocation contribute to performance.
The paper is generally well organized, includes pseudocode and complete prompt templates, reports inference cost, and discusses limitations and societal impact.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is moderate: the main contribution combines established KD-tree partitioning and UCB-style heuristics with an LLM sampler, without theoretical guarantees or a principled derivation of the composite score.

The synthetic evaluation does not use randomly shifted, rotated, or newly generated functions. LLMs may know canonical functions and optima from pretraining; the striking result of finding the standard Ackley-20D optimum near zero is therefore not convincing evidence of general black-box optimization ability.

Several reporting inconsistencies undermine confidence. Table 4 gives exactly identical results for GP-EI, regularized evolution, and random search on all three tasks; the text claims broadly consistent superiority although HOLLM loses to the global LLM on Rosenbrock in that table and performs poorly on Rastrigin; the manuscript also alternates between 'iterations' and function evaluations despite batched evaluation.

Statistical evidence is incomplete. Curves show standard errors, but there are no per-task significance tests or full numerical results for the main experiments, and some prominent appendix conclusions rely on only three to six repetitions.

Reproducibility is currently insufficient: the promised repository link is empty, important LLM inference settings such as sampling temperature and exact model/API versions are not specified, and proprietary-model nondeterminism is not characterized.

Some analyses overstate their conclusions. The claimed robustness mechanism is described as restricting context locally even though the method supplies global history; the calibration results are imported from a follow-up paper and sometimes favor the global LLM; and the asymptotic comparison with Gaussian processes ignores incremental GP updates and the enormous constants of LLM inference. These issues make the empirical case promising but not yet fully reliable at a top-tier acceptance threshold.
